findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script to sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: The added line downloads a remote script and executes it immediately with no integrity verification: no pinned version/tag, no SHA256 check, no signature, and -L follows redirects so the final content can come from anywhere. Any compromise of the URL or its redirect chain becomes arbitrary code executed at image build time (inside the build context, with build-time secrets/env available). curl also runs without -f, so an HTTP error status is not propagated — the error page body is what gets executed. Current impact is latent (example.com is an IANA-reserved placeholder and the build already fails before any payload runs), which is why this is P2, not P1; it becomes critical the moment the placeholder is swapped for a real URL.

findings.title: Replace example.com placeholder URL: image build will fail
findings.whyItBreaks: example.com is an IANA-reserved placeholder domain and serves no install.sh; the request returns 404. curl without -f exits 0 on the HTTP 404 response, so the non-empty 404 page body is piped into sh, which cannot parse it and exits non-zero, failing the RUN step and deterministically breaking the Docker build. If the placeholder is ever replaced by a real-looking URL this also masks fetch failures via the missing -f.

findings.title: Make LoadOrDefault propagate the error or take an explicit default
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault ignores the error returned by Load (src/store.go:16) and returns the zero value on failure. Load's only error path is ErrMissing (src/store.go:10), so a missing key is mapped to "" — which is indistinguishable from a key that legitimately maps to the empty string (m["k"] = ""). This is an exported/public API with no in-repo callers yet, so the defect is the contract itself: any eventual caller that reads a key via LoadOrDefault cannot tell "unset" from "set to empty", and no caller can obtain any default other than "". Per the swallow rule this is a present defect, not speculation about future callers.

findings.title: Restore synchronous delivery or add a join mechanism in Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run delivered every j*2 to results before returning; the natural consumer contract was 'when Run returns, all values are sent' (safe to close(results) afterward, complete results available). The diff spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately, before any send happens. The function name Run and its signature (no WaitGroup, no returned done channel, ctx still ignored) still promise that calling Run performs the run, but the body no longer does: (1) a consumer that follows the old barrier pattern Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results) now races the goroutines — a send on the closed channel panics or values are dropped; (2) a consumer that reads fewer than len(jobs) values (e.g., stops on ctx.Done or a timeout) leaves unbuffered-channel senders blocked forever — goroutine leak; (3) any caller relying on results being populated when Run returns now reads stale/empty state. Exported carrier, body changed while the promise stayed — the promise affects exactly the data a caller receives (completion and timing of all results), so per the exported-carrier rule this is a present defect even with no in-repo caller.

findings.title: Restore tenant-scope check in canDeleteRecord (&& -> || bypasses tenantId)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, deletion required BOTH session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. After the change, canDeleteRecord({isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'}, {tenantId:'B'}) returns true, so a tenant-A admin can delete records owned by tenant B — the tenant-isolation comparison the function exists to enforce is bypassed for every admin session. This is cross-tenant record deletion (data loss + broken authorization boundary) and a silent widening of an exported authorization API with no supporting change anywhere in the repo. The only remaining justification would be 'admins are global', but the old code deliberately scoped even admins to their tenant, and no test, doc, or caller in this PR evidences that intent.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and silently persists defaults over corrupt settings
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: the new catch maps every failure (invalid JSON, non-string theme, non-number fontSize — including partial settings like {"theme":"dark"}) to DEFAULTS, discarding the error that previously reached the caller via throw. parseSettings is exported, so every external caller is forced to conflate 'corrupt settings' with 'defaults'. Concretely in-repo: updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) calls parseSettings(raw) and unconditionally save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22 — a corrupt raw string that previously aborted the save now gets overwritten with {theme:"light", fontSize:<new>}, destroying the prior persisted settings content and any chance of recovery; the user's theme preference is silently reset whenever fontSize is invalid while theme was valid.

findings.title: Align artifacts provenance with builtFrom in buildReport
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported BuildReport contract pairs builtFrom (the commit the report says the build came from) with artifacts; base code fetched both from the same commit (builtFrom: commit, artifactsAt(commit)). Head now sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but artifacts from build.ref("verified"), a different commit whenever branch != "verified". Any consumer of this exported API that attributes the artifact list to builtFrom (display, storage, downstream verification) receives mislabeled data — the report silently changes what artifacts belong to while keeping the builtFrom field that promises coherence. No Build implementation or 'verified' ref exists in this repo, so on a branch ref the artifact list is simply detached from the commit the report claims it was built from.

findings.title: Restore limit cap in recentEntries: return sorted.slice(0, limit)
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with a guard that only handles limit <= 0 and then returns the full reversed array. `limit` is no longer used for any positive value, so `recentEntries(all, 20)` returns all entries, not at most 20. The unchanged doc comment (line 1) still promises 'at most `limit` entries' — TRIGGER C contract drift. Relying caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9-12) sizes `out` to 20 and loops `for (i < page.length) out[i] = page[i]`; with all.length > 20 the array is extended past its intended 20-slot page and the whole feed is returned (and with all.length > 20, entries beyond the 20-slot page are silently returned as a growing page), so any feed consumer now renders the full feed instead of the newest 20.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries out of `rows` but still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines` (line 22). With any stale entry, the generated manifest header `# entry-count: N` overstates the number of rows actually present (e.g. entries=[{stale:true},{stale:false}] emits `# entry-count: 2` followed by 1 row; all-stale input emits `# entry-count: N` with zero rows). `renderManifest` is exported and the manifest is a persisted artifact, so any consumer that reads entry-count to validate completeness, size buffers, or iterate rows now receives a self-contradictory document; before this change count always equaled row count. The body change silently broke the existing carrier promise in headerLines (src/manifest.ts:15).

findings.title: Restore execute() to return a value; it now always throws
findings.whyItBreaks: The body was replaced with `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every call to this exported function crashes instead of returning the computed string. The unchanged signature `execute(input: string): string` (line 1) promises a string result that the body can never deliver — the function is now 100% non-functional for every caller, and no code path (no input, no condition) can succeed. No in-repo callers exist (grep finds only the definition), but this is a public exported API whose result is unconditionally replaced by a thrown error, so the defect ships to every external consumer now.

findings.title: Remove viewer rejection in isEligible: it blocks handle()'s read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible() now returns false for role==="viewer", and the only call site, handle() (src/handler.ts:24), returns "rejected" on that false. But handle() has an explicit branch for exactly this case: if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only" (src/handler.ts:25). Under base, an active viewer with attempts < 5 was eligible and handle() returned "read-only"; after this change it returns "rejected" and line 25 is unreachable dead code. The changed predicate rejects an action (read-only processing) that the caller treats as legitimately approvable, i.e. TRIGGER A over-block on a live path: same predicate now mis-governs the one action that reads it.

findings.title: payment gate in canProceed over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by both submitOrder and saveDraft. The added `order.payment === "paid"` conjunct now makes saveDraft return "blocked" for any order with payment==="missing", including drafts: `canProceed({state:"draft", payment:"missing"})` was true before this change ("saved") and is now false ("blocked"). Saving a draft of an unpaid order is legitimately approvable on its own — payment status is unrelated to the draft-save action — so this is a P2 regression in the save-draft workflow, not just a tightened submit precondition.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from "stable" ref while commit/channel refer to the requested channel
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces files: repo.filesAt(head) with files: repo.filesAt(stable) where stable = repo.headCommit("stable"), while commit/channel still refer to the requested channel's head. Whenever the requested channel's head differs from the "stable" ref head (the normal case — the function exists precisely to snapshot arbitrary channels), the returned Snapshot carries commit/channel from one commit and files from a different commit. Any consumer that persists, diffs, sizes, or deploys files as the content of commit (or of channel) silently records/publishes the wrong file set with no error. It is also silent: no validation catches commit vs files divergence. This is an exported public function, so the inconsistent contract is the defect even though this repo has no in-repo callers (verified: publishSnapshot is referenced nowhere else).

findings.title: Wire the new `limit` parameter into the loop instead of ignoring it
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds a public parameter `limit=10` to `build()` whose name promises the result is capped at `limit`, but the body never reads it: `max_count = 10` at line 2 and `range(max_count)` at line 4 are unchanged, so `build("x", limit=3)` returns 10 items instead of 3. This is TRIGGER C (contract drift): the carrier is the public parameter itself, and the promised behavior (capping) directly changes the data a caller receives, so it is a defect even with no in-repo caller yet. Every caller that passes a limit below 10 gets silently wrong-sized output with no error.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises positive validation the body does not implement
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename read_int -> parse_positive_int makes the public function name a contract carrier promising positivity validation, but the body is still `return int(value)`. Substituting a negative or zero input: parse_positive_int('-5') -> -5 (no rejection), so charge('-5') -> -500 and total_cents yields negative totals. Any caller who trusts the 'positive' promise and skips their own check receives and may persist/bill a negative amount. The name is the only validation surface here; it is a lie to every consumer.

findings.title: Restore df.copy() to stop in-place mutation of caller data
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `result = df.copy()` and writes through `df.loc[...] = value` on the caller's frame. The base version (git show 5892d82) returned a new frame and left the argument untouched; the signature/name are unchanged, so every existing caller of this public function keeps the old expectation but now silently has its input mutated. Any caller that reuses `df` after the call (further pipeline steps, persistence, comparison with the pre-call state) receives corrupted/overwritten data with no error. If `df` is itself a slice/view of another frame, the in-place write also triggers pandas SettingWithCopyWarning. The mask computation is unchanged, so this is purely a dropped defensive copy.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items): it moves `items` and breaks compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: std's `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => ... }`, which takes its operand by value. `Vec<String>` is not Copy, so `dbg!(items)` moves `items` out of the function scope; the very next statement `let total = items.len();` (src/store.rs:3) then borrows a moved value and fails to compile with E0382 "use of moved value: `items`". The crate — whose only source module is this file — deterministically fails to build; any consumer or test build is broken.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against the same revision as fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged carrier (exported Changeset doc at src/changeset.ts:6-8) promises: 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' The body now sets fromRevision=store.resolve(pinnedTag) but changedPaths=store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). For any store where pinnedTag != "latest" (the entire point of a pinned tag), the changed-path list is the diff (latest..tip), not the diff (pinnedTag..tip): every path changed between the pinned tag and latest that was not touched again after latest is silently dropped from the changeset, and a consumer replaying on top of fromRevision applies a path list computed against a different base — wrong/missing file set. Behavior is only correct in the degenerate case pinnedTag == "latest". TRIGGER C: promise (changedPaths computed against fromRevision, affects data the caller receives) != body (computed against latest); the carrier is exported/public, so this is a P2 even with no in-repo caller.

findings.title: Rename users.email breaks existing src/query.sql consumer
findings.whyItBreaks: After 0002 runs, the repo's only data-access statement src/query.sql:1 (SELECT email FROM users;) references a column that no longer exists; every execution errors (SQLite: 'no such column: email', Postgres: 'column users.email does not exist'). The rename is not propagated to the pre-existing consumer, so this is migration/upgrade breakage of a live path, not a benign rename. No other file references contact_email (verified with git grep at head), confirming the rename is one-sided.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key; restore env-var config and rotate the leaked secret
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces the BILLING_API_KEY env lookup (with its missing-config guard) with a literal credential "bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0". The bk_live_ prefix marks it as a production/live key, so this commits a live credential into the repo and its permanent git history (commit ad8f984). Any reader of the repo — or of any future fork/export — can authenticate as the billing account and trigger charges. It also pins every environment (dev/staging/prod) to the same live key: the removed throw means misconfiguration is now masked, and staging runs would bill against the live account with no per-environment isolation or rotation path.

findings.title: Invert admin guard in purgeProject: non-admins can delete, admins are blocked
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code purged iff user.isAdmin && project.archived (git show 43a2c3a:src/projects.ts:12). The restructure inverted the admin predicate: line 12 now returns "forbidden" for admins, so the purge path is only reachable when isAdmin is false. Substituting: user.isAdmin=true, project.archived=true -> returns "forbidden" (base returned "purged": legit admin action rejected); user.isAdmin=false, project.archived=true -> passes both guards, db.delete(project.id) runs and returns "purged" (base returned "forbidden": non-admin now gains delete authority over archived projects). Both directions of the permission contract are wrong: admins lose a legitimately approvable action (TRIGGER A) and non-admins gain a delete capability that base explicitly denied. The function is an exported public API, so this ships a broken authorization contract even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore missing-config default in startup() or fail with a clear error
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() explicitly returns None when the config file does not exist (app/config.py:6-7), and that is the exact case the removed guard handled. With the guard gone, a missing config path now evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, instead of returning the previous default workers=1. The fallback branch was a designed behavior for a reachable input, so deleting it converts a graceful default into a crash for anyone calling startup() with a missing/invalid path.

findings.title: Propagate gw.Submit error instead of logging and returning nil
findings.whyItBreaks: On submit failure the function now logs the error and falls through to `return nil` — the exact same value as the success path. `Charge` is exported and its `error` return contract promises failure propagation (`charge failed: %w` before this change); any caller doing `if err := Charge(...); err != nil` will treat a failed charge as successful and may record the payment as complete or skip retry, while the actual charge was never submitted. Failure and the nil fallback are indistinguishable at every decision point, so the log line does not rescue the contract.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in the settings cache key to avoid cross-tenant cache collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: The new cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` and the lookup at line 12 ignores tenantId. On a live path: settingsFor(tenantA, "feature", store) populates cache["settings:feature"]; a later settingsFor(tenantB, "feature", store) hits that entry (line 14) and returns tenant A's value to tenant B without ever calling store.fetch(tenantB, ...). Every tenant requesting the same setting name is served the first tenant's cached value — wrong settings are routed across tenants, and per-tenant fetch/invalidation semantics are silently lost.

findings.title: Restore the (tenantId, name) signature of exported invalidate()
findings.whyItBreaks: invalidate is an exported API whose signature changed from (tenantId, name) to (name). Any existing caller passing two arguments now fails to compile, and a one-argument call can no longer scope invalidation to a tenant — after the cache-key fix, invalidate(name) could delete another tenant's entry. The public contract was broken by this PR with no in-repo callers updated (there are none in the repo).

findings.title: Fix TOCTOU: concurrent reserve() calls can oversell stock after adding await
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() now reads remaining (line 15), suspends at `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17), and only then updates this.stock (line 18). Two concurrent reserve('A') calls with stock=1 both observe remaining=1 before either updates the map, both persist 0, both set stock to 0, and both return true — 2 reservations granted for 1 unit. The pre-change body was fully synchronous and atomic within one event-loop turn, so the await introduces the race. This is the class's core reservation path: oversell is a wrong persisted result (the save wrote 0 twice, so the external store also records oversold state, not just the in-memory map).

findings.title: Changing reserve() from boolean to Promise<boolean> silently breaks existing consumers
findings.whyItBreaks: The public method's return type changed from boolean to Promise<boolean> (line 14). A caller compiled against the old signature doing `if (this.inventory.reserve(sku)) { ship }` still typechecks (Promise<boolean> is truthy-checkable) but now always takes the true branch — including the `if (remaining <= 0) return false` path (line 16), which yields Promise<false>, also truthy. Empty-stock reservations silently proceed as if granted. The class is exported and this is a hard API break with no compile-time or runtime signal to un-migrated callers; the failure is indistinguishable from success.

findings.title: Update retry.ts consumer: backoff now returns ms, sleep delays 1000× too long
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changes backoff() from seconds (min(30, 2**a)) to milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**a * 1000)) and updates only poll.ts. The second consumer src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still computes sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), which is now (ms) * 1000 = seconds*1000: attempt 0 slept 1s, now sleeps ~16.7min; attempt 4 slept 16s, now ~4.4h; the 30s cap became a 30,000s (~8.3h) cap. A retry job that used to finish its worst-case backoff window in ~30s per attempt now stalls up to ~8.3h per attempt (sleep is awaited inside the loop at retry.ts:12, so the whole retry workflow is held open, likely under its caller's deadline). Silent regression: no error, no log change.

findings.title: Restore propagation of f.Close() error in Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code ended with `return f.Close()`, so any error from the final close (NFS deferred write errors, quota/ENOSPC reported at close, EIO on flush-to-disk) reached the caller and Save returned non-nil. The new code replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (error discarded) and `return w.Flush()`. A close failure now yields a nil return: callers cannot distinguish 'saved' from 'not persisted'. Save is an exported public API of the store package, so this is a present contract defect even though no in-repo caller exists yet; a silent-close-failure on a save path risks reporting data as durably written when it was not. (Write ordering is otherwise correct — Flush runs before the deferred Close — so the only dropped signal is the close error.)

findings.title: Fix page_window range to include end-1 (last row of each page is dropped)
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code did `range(start, end)`; the new loop `for position in range(start, end - 1)` stops at end-2, so the last row of every window is excluded. Substitution: rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_size=2 -> page 0 bounds (0,2) yields [a] (b lost), page 1 (2,4) yields [c] (d lost), page 2 (4,5) yields [] (e lost). A page holding exactly one row renders empty. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) are the direct consumers, so every rendered page and the final page of summarize output silently lose rows, and the 1-based line numbers skip (e.g. '1. a' then '3. c'). The page_window docstring "Rows belonging to page_index" promises full page contents; the body does not implement it.

findings.title: Restore TTL comparison in TtlCache.get: fresh entries are evicted, expired entries served
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Substituting real values: set('k','v') stores storedAt=Date.now(); a get 1ms later gives age=1ms; with ttlMs=60000, `1 > 60000` is false, so the code falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` — a fresh, valid entry is evicted and reported as a miss on its first read. Conversely, an entry older than ttlMs (age 120000) satisfies `120000 > 60000` and its stale value is returned as valid. The cache now does the exact opposite of its contract: live data returns null, expired data returns a value. Every consumer of the exported TtlCache gets inverted semantics, and repeated gets of fresh keys churn the map.

findings.title: Iterate pruneDone backwards: splice during forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting concrete values: jobs=[{id:'a',done:true},{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}]. index 0: 'a' is done -> splice(0,1) shifts 'b' to index 0, array is now [b,c]. index 1: 'c' is not done, kept. Result [b(done), c] — job 'b', which is done, is returned by pruneDone. For [a(done), b(done)] the result is [b(done)] instead of []. forEach iterates by live length and index, so every splice makes the loop skip the next element. The exported pruneDone no longer prunes all done jobs, so callers enqueueing or scheduling from its result will process finished jobs.

findings.title: Restore non-mutating pruneDone: in-place splice destroys the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used `jobs.filter(...)`, which returned a new array and left the input untouched. The replacement mutates the input array in place (splice) and returns the same reference. Any caller that reads `jobs` after calling pruneDone — re-reading the queue, iterating it elsewhere, or having passed a shared array — now sees done jobs removed from their own array, and the returned array is the caller's array (aliased), not a new one. This is a silent contract change on an exported public function: same signature, different semantics for the caller's data.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator: bare sort() sorts scores as strings, breaking top-N selection
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator sorts elements as UTF-16 strings, not numbers. scores.sort() on [9,10,8] yields [10,8,9]; after reverse() the array is [9,8,10] (not [10,9,8]). Substituting into the live path: players=[{a,9},{b,10},{c,8}], n=3 → cutoff=scores[Math.min(3,3)-1]=scores[2]=10 → filter(score>=10) returns only [{b,10}], so topPlayers returns 1 of 3 players and formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:19-22) prints a wrong, truncated board. Base commit sorted with (a,b)=>b-a, a correct numeric descending sort; this diff regresses every call of the exported topPlayers for any score set with mixed digit lengths.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates the webhook's only authentication: handle() returns 401 unless verify() is true, then runs processor(payload) on attacker-supplied payload (app/webhook.py:14-16). The change replaces hmac.compare_digest with '==' (app/webhook.py:10), which short-circuits at the first mismatched character, so runtime is proportional to the matching prefix length. A remote attacker can measure response timing (amplified by the 401 vs 200 branch, plus the digest comparison itself) to recover the expected HMAC prefix byte-by-byte, forge a valid signature without the secret, and invoke processor() with arbitrary payloads — a classic CWE-208 signature-forgery path. Comparison results are otherwise identical, so no test that checks True/False will catch it.

findings.title: Move _apply_balances back inside the db.transaction() block
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor moved the two balance UPDATEs out of the transaction. In base, the ledger INSERT, debit, and credit all committed or rolled back as one unit. Now the ledger INSERT commits first (line 23), then _apply_balances runs with no transaction (line 24). The two UPDATEs are no longer atomic with each other or with the ledger row: if the credit UPDATE (balance + cents, line 14-16) fails after the debit succeeded, from_acct is permanently debited while to_acct is never credited, and the committed ledger row records a transfer that never completed — funds silently vanish with no rollback path. Any statement-level error between the debit and credit (constraint, disk error, timeout) produces the same inconsistent, persisted state.

findings.title: Use UTC getters in billingDay; local-time day key varies by timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so billingDay now returns the process's local calendar day instead of the UTC day. For any instant whose local date differs from its UTC date (true for every nonzero timezone offset during part of the day), the returned key changes: e.g. 2026-08-01T20:00:00Z yields '2026-08-01' under TZ=UTC but '2026-08-02' under TZ=Asia/Tokyo. The key therefore differs per host/process timezone for the same instant, and sameBillingDay comparisons can flip depending on the runtime environment — events/usage get attributed to different billing days depending on where the code runs, and any persisted or server-computed UTC-based keys no longer match. billingDay is a public export; the base (40b9168) implementation established the UTC contract, and the unchanged signature promises a deterministic canonical day for an instant while the body no longer delivers it.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key: account-only key collides across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo is module-level (src/profile.ts:7) and the key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` (src/profile.ts:14). readProfile still takes both tenant and account and the returned Profile carries a tenant field, so readProfile('t1','acct') followed by readProfile('t2','acct') returns t1's cached profile (tenant 't1') for the t2 request — silently wrong data and a cross-tenant information bleed, with no error raised. The base version keyed on both fields; the diff removes that guarantee.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key errors in exported load()
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw `missing: ${key}` when a key was absent, letting callers distinguish 'key not found' from a legitimate stored value. The new catch-all converts every failure (missing key, or any error thrown by store.get) into "", which is a valid value in a Map<string,string>. Any caller validating required keys, routing on presence, or reporting missing config now silently receives "" and cannot tell a real empty value from a lookup failure; loadAll() inherits the same conflation for every element. Because load is an exported API, every external caller is forced into this conflation even though no in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Renaming exported Config.timeoutMs to timeout breaks every existing retry() consumer with no migration path
findings.whyItBreaks: Config and retry are exported public API. Removing timeoutMs and making the replacement timeout a required field (plus a required retries field) breaks every existing caller: TS consumers fail to compile (missing required timeout/retries, excess timeoutMs); JS/untyped consumers silently get deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN, and since Date.now() > NaN is always false (src/retry.ts:10), the deadline guard never rejects and timeout enforcement silently disappears — all maxAttempts run with no time bound. Old callers break either loudly (compile) or silently (deadline disabled), with no alias/deprecation.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry but reads a second required Config field (retries) that retry() ignores, and vice versa for maxAttempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a near-verbatim copy of retry (same deadline + catch-continue + return-on-success) whose only difference is reading config.retries (line 22) instead of config.maxAttempts (line 9). The shared exported Config now requires BOTH fields, and each function silently ignores the one it does not read: retry ignores retries, retryBackground ignores maxAttempts. A runtime caller of retryBackground that supplies only the established maxAttempts field (per the pre-existing retry API) hits i < undefined/0 → the loop never executes → fn() is never invoked, silently, with no error. The duplicate is also what forced the required-field split that breaks the API (finding 1).

findings.title: Render the actual value; length label and number handling are a regression
findings.whyItBreaks: Two defects in the same hunk. (1) Unrelated behavior change: the field previously rendered defaultValue={value}; it now renders `len=${value.length}`, so every form field shows 'len=5' instead of its real value — a user-visible rendering regression on every caller, almost certainly debug code committed by accident. (2) The type change to `value: string | number` is contradicted by the body: `value.length` is `undefined` for a number, so any number input renders 'len=undefined'. The widened exported FieldProps advertises numbers as valid while the implementation cannot render one.

findings.title: Do not echo the TOKEN secret into the workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step prints the value of secrets.TOKEN to the runner stdout via `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. GitHub's log masking is best-effort (it only redacts the exact secret value, and any transformation — truncation, encoding, whitespace-wrapping — defeats it), and this is a deploy workflow on every push with a credentials-bearing token; if masking ever misses (or logs are forwarded/archived to third-party services), the deploy credential is exposed to anyone with log read access. The secret is also never consumed by an actual deploy command here — the step only demonstrates the token rather than using it, so the echo carries no functional value and only adds exposure. This is the classic anti-pattern GitHub itself documents against: never print secrets in workflow logs.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer in git(): diffs over 1 MiB now fail with an empty error
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024 (1 MiB). git() is called with `git diff mergeBase headSha` at line 140, which emits the full PR patch; any PR touching a lockfile, vendored dir, or generated code can exceed 1 MiB. On overflow Node kills the child and sets res.error (code ENOBUFS) with res.status === null and res.stdout/stderr === null. The unchanged guard `res.status !== 0` then throws `git <args> failed: ` with an empty message (stderr is null), masking the real cause. The throw happens at line 140, before the try/catch at line 176, so no failure check-run is posted and the review silently never happens for PRs that worked before. gh() and ghText() still set 64 MiB, indicating the removal is accidental.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox flag on the codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `-s read-only` from the args passed to `spawnSync(bin, args, { cwd: opts.repoPath, ... })`. `codex exec -s` selects the sandbox policy for model-generated shell commands (verified: possible values read-only / workspace-write / danger-full-access), and when the flag is omitted the CLI falls back to its default/config sandbox (workspace-write), which the base commit was explicitly pinning away. `runCodex` executes an externally supplied `prompt` (agent-generated, i.e. untrusted) with cwd set to the caller's repoPath; under the base behavior the executed agent could not persist any file changes, whereas now it can modify, create, or delete files inside repoPath (and run arbitrary shell commands with those permissions). This removes the security boundary that protected the reviewed repository from the code under evaluation and introduces a data-loss surface on every caller of this exported function, including ones outside this repo.

findings.title: Restore headSha and merge-base in diff range; HEAD/raw baseSha break env overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha is still resolved from PR_HEAD_SHA at github.ts:137 and posted as the review commit_id (postReview github.ts:178 -> payload commit_id github.ts:85, check head_sha github.ts:179/185), but the patch and changed-file set now use literal "HEAD" and raw baseSha. When PR_HEAD_SHA is set to a commit different from the checked-out HEAD (the configuration the env var exists for, e.g. checkout of a merge ref), the reviewed diff is computed against HEAD while being attached to headSha: findings and inline comment line positions (side RIGHT, github.ts:66-67) come from HEAD's diff, which GitHub's review API rejects for commit headSha (positions not in its diff), triggering the fallback in postReview (github.ts:96-109) that silently drops ALL inline comments and posts only the summary body. Separately, dropping merge-base(baseSha, headSha) means a diverged PR_BASE_SHA (base tip, not merge-base) now pollutes the range with the base branch's own changes: changedPaths (github.ts:141) includes files the PR never touched, so findings on those files get posted against headSha and rejected/dropped the same way. The old code was consistent in every configuration (merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha matched the posted commit_id).

findings.title: Restore function replacers; string replace corrupts prompts when bundle/patch contains $
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets the replacement STRING as a substitution template (GetSubstitution) but inserts a function's return value literally. With the new string arguments: $$ -> $, $& -> the matched placeholder ('{{BUNDLE}}'/'{{PATCH}}'), $' -> the template text AFTER the placeholder, $` -> the template text before it, and $n -> the nth capture (empty or literal when absent). So any '$'-prefixed sequence in JSON.stringify(bundle) (agentsMd/prMeta are arbitrary text), JSON.stringify(candidate) (LLM output), or bundle.patch (raw git diff text, routinely contains $&/$$/$' in shell, sed/awk, string literals) silently deletes content or injects template text into the prompt sent to runCodex (review.ts:25, review.ts:33). Verified by executing the exact semantics: template "T {{BUNDLE}} E" + title "PR $& and $1 and $'x and $$" renders "PR {{BUNDLE}} and $1 and  Ex and $ E" ($& injected the placeholder, $' pulled ' E' across the closing quote, $$ collapsed to $); control with the function replacer preserved every character verbatim. The old code at base (function form) preserved all of it literally, so this PR regresses the prompt-building path.

findings.title: Restore commit_id pin in fallback review post to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary post (lines 88-99) pins commit_id=headSha, but the fallback (lines 100-113) now omits it. The GitHub REST API documents that an omitted commit_id "defaults to the most recent commit in the pull request". postReview runs after the full LLM review (runGithub line 183), and headSha is captured at checkout (line 141); if the PR head advances during the review (or PR_HEAD_SHA points at a non-head commit), the fallback review - including a REQUEST_CHANGES/pass verdict - is recorded against a commit that was never reviewed, producing a false review record in the PR. The fallback fires whenever the primary gh --input call throws, which is exactly the error path this code runs on. Restoring the flag costs nothing and keeps the pin in the pinned-valid case (GitHub accepts any commit in the PR), so the removal only adds misattribution without fixing a failure mode except the force-push case, where a failed check would be more honest than a misattributed verdict.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-finding errors, fabricating default findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Base contract (verified via git show 2cbebd1): normalizeReview defaulted strict=true and normalizeFinding threw on missing/invalid severity, category, title, file, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, or non-positive line numbers, so the caller could reject the whole review output (retry / needs_human) when a finding was malformed. The diff deletes every per-finding check and the strict flag: a finding with missing or invalid fields is now coerced to severity 'P1', category 'bug', title 'Untitled finding', file '' and lineStart/lineEnd 0, and the fabricated finding flows out of the public normalizeReview (line 131 map) as if it were real. Failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate value, so consumers persist/report/annotate fabricated findings; the 'Untitled finding' with file ''/lineStart 0 even violates the Finding type's own guarantees (file is non-optional, lineStart > 0 was enforced). Both functions are exported, so the defect ships now even though no in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: Stop swallowing malformed review output into an all-clear empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: the old body threw descriptive errors ('malformed review output: not an object / summary missing / findings missing / checked missing / residual_risks missing') so a caller could distinguish a broken model response from a valid review. The new body discards every one of those signals: null/non-object input, missing or non-string summary, and missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks are all defaulted to summary:'' + [] . The result is indistinguishable from a legitimate zero-finding review: a harness that submits, persists, or reports the normalized review will treat a malformed run as a clean PASS with no findings, instead of retrying or flagging needs_human as the thrown error previously forced. Since normalizeReview is exported (public contract) and the swallow is total (no logging, no marker), the defect ships even with no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: Restore PR base/head SHA resolution on workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only source of base/head values on workflow_dispatch (it ran `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json baseRefOid/headRefOid/baseRef`). On workflow_dispatch the event payload has no pull_request object, so `${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` and `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` evaluate to empty strings and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA reach src/cli.ts empty. The same gap breaks the checkout: `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` (line 29) falls back to the dispatch branch (typically main), not the PR head, and 'Fetch base branch' (line 35) defaults BASE_REF to 'main' even when the PR's base is another branch. A manual dispatch therefore reviews the wrong tree and hands the CLI an empty diff base instead of the PR's SHAs — the documented manual-trigger path regresses. (No in-repo consumer of the SHAs exists — the repo contains only the workflow; the workflow-level regression is fully observable in this file.)

findings.title: Restore 64MB maxBuffer on git() — 1MB default kills large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1MB (1024*1024). When stdout exceeds it, Node kills the child, res.status becomes null, and res.error is ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER. The guard at local.ts:12 (`res.status !== 0`) then throws for a git command that legitimately succeeded. The largest consumer is local.ts:100 `git diff baseSha HEAD`, whose output is unbounded by the repo size — a PR patch over ~1MB (lockfile bumps, generated files, large refactors, which this tool exists to review) now aborts runLocal with an opaque `git diff <base> HEAD failed:` message and an empty stderr. Previously the 64MB cap (which gh() at local.ts:36 still has) supported these diffs. The failure also downgrades the error signal: the misleading empty-stderr throw hides the actual cause (buffer overflow) since res.error is not surfaced.

findings.title: Report review-failure check run as neutral, unblocking merges and conflating error with needs_human verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path of runGithub (github.ts:185-197) posts a check run with conclusion "neutral" (changed from "failure") whenever review() or the API calls throw. GitHub branch protection treats a check with conclusion neutral as PASSED, so a PR whose review errored out is now mergeable even though the summary text (github.ts:193) still states "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." The failure signal is also no longer distinguishable from the legitimate needs_human verdict, which intentionally maps to neutral (VERDICT_CONCLUSION, github.ts:53): branch protection sees identical state for a tool crash and a "needs human" verdict, so the review gate is silently disabled exactly on the path that produces no verdict. process.exitCode = 1 only fails the Actions job step; consumers of the check-run conclusion (the branch-protection merge gate) only see neutral = pass.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; self-review lets the PR control its own review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow deliberately split tool from target: it checked out frankekn/needlefish@main (trusted main) into needlefish/ and ran its src/cli.ts against the PR head checked out into target/ (see f412512:32-42). The new workflow runs pnpm install on the PR head's own package.json (line 51) and executes the PR head's own src/cli.ts (line 59) as the reviewer, with GITHUB_TOKEN scoped to pull-requests: write and checks: write (lines 18-19). Any same-repo PR (the job's if-guard at line 24 allows all same-repo PRs, and the workflow file itself already runs for them) can now modify src/cli.ts or inject a dependency via package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml and have the reviewer check/comment/approve exactly what it wants — the 'PR controls its own review' integrity property the removed comment and the old two-checkout pattern explicitly existed to prevent. The new comment's justification ('this repo IS needlefish') doesn't hold: the old pattern already worked for the tool's own repo (frankekn/needlefish@main is the same repo's trusted main), so self-review is a strict integrity downgrade with no functional gain — every future needlefish PR touching src/ is now reviewed by its own modified code, and the review check conclusion is forgeable by the code under review.

findings.title: Point the comment at README.md template that does not exist in this repo
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed comment promises 'For OTHER repos, use the generic template in README.md (which adds a second checkout of frankekn/needlefish as the tool)'. Verified at HEAD: git ls-tree shows the repo contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json — there is no README.md anywhere. The only documented path back to the secure two-checkout pattern is a broken pointer; any repo that copies this workflow silently ships self-review with no recovery instructions.

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: SEVERITIES is exactly ['P0','P1','P2','P3'] (schema.ts:85), and the only caller is normalizeReview (schema.ts:132), which feeds raw LLM JSON (raw: any) through normalizeFinding. The base code coerced raw.severity with String(...).trim().toUpperCase() before the includes check; the new code compares the raw value directly, so any case/whitespace variant the model emits ('p0', 'p1', ' P2 ', numeric) fails SEVERITIES.includes and is silently mapped to 'P3' — the lowest severity — instead of its intended P0/P1/P2. A lowercase 'p0' now surfaces as P3, misclassifying priority in the review output. The fallback default was also changed from 'P1' to 'P3', so a missing/unknown severity is now recorded as lowest priority instead of P1. Both changes compound on the same path: every unrecognized severity lands on P3.

findings.title: Restore stripping GitHub tokens from codex subprocess environment
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version deliberately deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN from the environment before spawning codex; this PR removes that block and the `env` option, so spawnSync now inherits process.env wholesale (codex.ts:23-29). The child is a third-party binary (`process.env.CODEX_BIN ?? "codex"`, codex.ts:13) that spawns agent/tool subprocesses in the repo; all of them can read the inherited tokens directly or via /proc/<pid>/environ and can exfiltrate them through transcripts/logs or use them for authenticated GitHub calls as the user. Removing this credential boundary with no compensating control is a security regression; there is no behavioral fix the stripping was blocking (env is only used to launch the child).

findings.title: Restore fork-repo guard: untrusted fork PRs run arbitrary code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` removes the only fork filter: `on: pull_request` fires for fork PRs (review.yml:8), and the job now unconditionally checks out the PR head (review.yml:23) and executes `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (runs package.json pre/postinstall scripts from the PR) plus the PR's own `src/cli.ts` (review.yml:34) on a self-hosted runner. A malicious fork author therefore gets arbitrary code execution on the persistent runner host (potentially holding credentials, other repo checkouts, host access) — precisely the attack the removed guard is GitHub's documented defense for. Secondary: fork PRs receive a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, so the declared `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` permissions (review.yml:13-14) are ignored for them and the review cannot post its results anyway.

findings.title: Restore >= 0: '0' grace/give-up setting silently falls back to 5000/2000ms
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting parsed=0: guard `parsed > 0` @135 rejects it, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now yields RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=5000 instead of 0, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 yields 2000 instead of 0. 0 is a legitimate, meaningful value for both knobs: grace=0 means SIGKILL immediately when the timeout fires (hardKillTimer @117-124 fires 5s later than configured), and give-up=0 means resolve finish() right after SIGKILL instead of waiting up to 2s for 'close' on a runner whose escapee keeps pipes open (@119-123). A user setting 0 to bound hang time gets the opposite extreme, silently, so the misconfiguration is undetectable. Impact is confined to operators explicitly setting these two env vars; the base commit (which added the whole file) accepted 0, and nothing in-repo (no docs, no tests) documents 0 as invalid, so the rejection is an unannounced semantic change. Caveat: the module is unreleased and the edit is a deliberate one-char hardening, so the author may have intended to reject 0.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop so unmapped changed files still get deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block (base lines 98-110) explicitly guaranteed 'never silently skip a changed file': any changed file not assigned to a hotspot by the map pass was pushed into a 'tail-coverage' hotspot and deep-reviewed. The map pass is a model-generated surface survey with no in-repo guarantee of exhaustiveness, and the removed code's own why-text ('these changed files were not assigned to any surface') proves unassigned files are a real, anticipated case. With the backstop gone, an unmapped changed file is never deep-reviewed, never appears in the checked[] list, and the review still returns a normal verdict — so reviewLarge can emit PASS while a changed file was never examined.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot failure handling so one failed deep pass cannot abort the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed try/catch (base lines 122-132) turned a per-hotspot runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview failure into a checked entry plus a blocks:true residual risk, and continued deep-reviewing the remaining hotspots. Now any single hotspot failure throws out of reviewLarge, discarding the map result and the findings/checked entries of every already-completed hotspot. runCodex is an external LLM call that can transiently fail (timeout, rate limit); a single such failure now converts a formerly partial-but-delivered review into a total abort with zero findings, whereas the base path delivered the other hotspots' findings plus an explicit 'not all files deep-reviewed' block signal.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-agent residual risks in the large-review pipeline
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: base collected residual_risks from every deep pass (base line 127) and the blocks:true coverage-failure entries (base line 131) into candidateMerged.residual_risks, where they reached the critic prompt ({{FINDINGS}}, base line 143) and could be carried into the returned ReviewResult.residualRisks. The change hard-codes residual_risks: [] (also dropping the ResidualRisk collection), so deep-agent unresolved/blocked items can never reach the critic or the final output: previously_reached=critic prompt + final ReviewResult.residualRisks, now_receives=[]. review() is exported and residualRisks is part of the public ReviewResult contract, so every eventual consumer is forced to conflate 'reviewed with no coverage gaps' with 'deep agents flagged blocked items' — the unusable contract is the defect. This also compounds the backstop removal: the only remaining signal that some files were not deep-reviewed is gone.

findings.title: Re-substitute {{FOCUS}} and restore focus/deep to large-PR prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Verified against the actual commit range 4333cdd..dacacf7: the diff is only 3 deletions in src/core/review.ts. Base code serialized focus/deep into mapBundle (old lines 89-90) and substituted {{FOCUS}} in the deep prompt (old line 122, confirmed via git show 4333cdd:src/core/review.ts). Head removes both: the map pass loses the fields, and the deep pass no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}}. The deleted .replace is direct evidence deep.md contained the placeholder at base, and since the diff touches no template, it still does at head — the literal text "{{FOCUS}}" now reaches the model in every deep pass. rg at head finds zero reads of bundle.focus/bundle.deep in src/, while reviewSmall (src/core/review.ts:51-56) still serializes the full bundle including focus/deep via JSON.stringify(bundle), so a user-supplied focus directive now silently does nothing on the large-PR path yet is still honored on the small path — the feature behaves differently by PR size with no error.

findings.title: Clamp seconds to 0-59 after rounding so formatDuration cannot emit "Xm 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) yields 60 whenever the remainder is in [59500, 60000) and minutes >= 1. E.g. ms=119999: minutes=1, seconds=round(59.999)=60 -> renders "1m 60s". The old code rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000) then mod 60), so it produced "2m 0s" for the same input and never emitted a carry. This is user-visible in the rendered review stats lines (render.ts:75 and render.ts:80), which pass arbitrary measured durationMs values.

findings.title: Align parsePositiveInteger with its contract: rejects only <0, accepts 0 despite name/message promising positive
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger (src/shared/runner.ts:30) and throws '${label} requires a positive integer' (src/shared/runner.ts:33), both of which promise that the returned value is strictly positive (>= 1) and that 0 is invalid input. The changed guard `parsed < 0` (was `parsed <= 0`) now lets 0 through, so any caller (or downstream validation built on this public helper) receives 0 where the carrier promises a positive integer, and the error text no longer describes the enforced rule. This is TRIGGER C contract drift on an exported symbol: the promised behavior is input validation that directly affects the result/data a caller receives, so the mismatch is a defect even with no current in-repo callers. If allowing 0 was intentional, the name and error message must change; otherwise the check must keep rejecting 0.
